Levodopa is the mainstay in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease (p.791) but opinion varies on when it should be used in the course of the disease. Most patients respond to levodopa initially but after a few years benefit may be reduced. There may be problems with dyskinesias and psychiatric effects and fluctuations in mobility necessitating careful dosage adjust- ment or the use of adjunctive drugs. For most patients treatment with levodopa eventually becomes necessary, but many neurolo- gists delay initial treatment with levodopa because of the in- creased risk of motor complications. New patients, especially younger patients, therefore often begin treatment with a dopamine agonist, with levodopa reserved for the elderly, the frail, or those with intercurrent illness or more severe symptoms. Levodopa should be given with a peripheral dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor; a peripheral catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor may also be necessary for patients experiencing fluctu- ations in disability related to levodopa and dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor combinations.
